On a recent trip down the dairy aisle of my local supermarket, I counted cartons of beverages derived from soybeans, almonds, oats, rice, and even peas. Plant-based milks, once a niche product for consumers who could not digest lactose, have become a commonplace purchase for many households. Buyers cite diverse motives: concern for animal welfare, an aspiration to shrink their environmental footprint, or simply a fondness for the taste in their coffee.
The boom has not been immune to controversy. Dairy farmers have contended that the word milk should be reserved for products of animals. In 2017 the European Union's top court sided with them, ruling that beverages made purely from plants generally may not be sold as milk within the bloc. In the United States the Food and Drug Administration proposed in 2023 that such drinks could keep the label but should disclose how their nutrients compare with those of cow's milk.
That comparison is far from trivial. Apart from soy drinks, many plant milks contain far less protein than dairy milk, and much of their calcium and vitamin content is added during manufacturing. Environmental claims also vary considerably by crop; almonds, for instance, are often criticized for the copious water needed to cultivate them.

If we plotted the personal memories of a seventy-year-old along a timeline, we might anticipate a smooth slope, with the most remote events faintest and the newest ones most abundant. Researchers who have done this with thousands of volunteers, asking each person to describe whatever episode a cue word evokes, find something peculiar. Recent years are indeed well represented and the first few years of life are virtually blank, yet a second peak towers over the stretch from about the age of ten to thirty. A similar peak manifests itself in the songs elderly people cherish most. Psychologists have dubbed it the reminiscence bump.
Why should youth claim so disproportionate a share? Part of the answer may be that those years abound with beginnings: the first paycheck, the first time living away from one's parents, the first romance. Events that break a routine are typically recalled in finer detail. Identity offers a second clue, because people at this juncture are settling what they value, and the episodes that shaped those choices get recounted for decades. Culture supplies a third. Communities transmit a common picture of when a life's pivotal chapters ought to begin, and <u>this script</u> steers what people look for in memory when asked to narrate their own past.

High in the Andes of southern Peru a footbridge woven entirely from grass hangs about thirty meters above the Apurimac River. Known as Q'eswachaka, it is the last surviving example of the rope bridges that once linked the vast road network of the Inca Empire. The bridge does not last long. Its grass fibers are battered by rain and sun, and within a year they begin to rot. For this reason the local Quechua communities take it down and build a new one every June. Each household gathers a native grass and twists it into thin cords, and the cords are then braided into thick cables as wide as a man's thigh, which are stretched across the gorge and anchored to stone abutments on either side.
The whole job takes only about three days. When the new bridge is finished, the old one is cut loose and allowed to fall into the river, where it decays harmlessly. The rebuilding is also a festival with music and offerings to the earth and the river. In 2013 UNESCO added the tradition to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. What endures is not the bridge itself but the knowledge and cooperation needed to remake it.

When work began on the Brooklyn Bridge around 1870, the foundations of its towers were dug inside caissons, colossal wooden chambers open at the bottom that were sunk into the riverbed. Compressed air was pumped in to keep out water and mud, and laborers worked in the pressurized space for hours at a stretch. After ascending to the surface, many of them developed excruciating pain in their joints, vertigo, and sometimes paralysis. Several died. Because no one comprehended the cause, the affliction was simply labeled caisson disease. Even the chief engineer Washington Roebling was incapacitated. He spent years directing the project from his room and relied on his wife Emily to convey his instructions to the site.
We now understand the mechanism. Under high pressure, surplus nitrogen dissolves into the blood and tissues. If the pressure is released too abruptly, the gas comes out of solution and forms bubbles, much as a bottle of soda fizzes when its cap is suddenly twisted off. The British physiologist John Scott Haldane devised a remedy in the early twentieth century. Divers and caisson workers were brought up in incremental stages so the gas could be expelled harmlessly through the lungs.

In 2021 researchers published one of the largest surveys to date of how young people feel about climate change. They questioned 10,000 people aged 16 to 25 in ten countries, from the Philippines to Finland. Most respondents said they were very or extremely worried, many described feeling despondent, apprehensive, powerless, or indignant, and large numbers said their governments were failing them.
The findings drew wider attention to what is often called climate anxiety or eco-anxiety. The term can sound like a diagnosis, but it is not listed as a mental disorder, and many psychologists warn against treating it as one. In their view, distress about a real and well-documented threat is a rational response rather than a symptom to be cured. Complications arise when worry becomes so overwhelming that it paralyzes people or disrupts their sleep, study, and relationships.
Counselors who work with anxious students often advocate two strategies. The first is to talk: young people frequently assume that the adults around them are indifferent, and discovering shared concern can alleviate the sense of isolation. The second is to act, whether by enlisting in a local project or altering a daily habit. Action does not make the problem vanish, but it can transform helplessness into something more tolerable.

Few writers have countered complaints about the brevity of life as bluntly as the Roman philosopher Seneca. In a first-century essay usually known in English as On the Shortness of Life he argued that the trouble is not that nature grants us too little time. Life, in his view, is ample for great achievements if it is prudently invested; it seems short only because we squander so much of it.
Seneca's inventory of wasted time is strikingly familiar. He describes people who spend their days waiting on influential patrons, pursuing fortunes they never pause to savor, or rushing from one frivolous diversion to the next. Such people guard their money and land jealously yet surrender their hours to anyone who asks. They act as if time were the one thing that cost nothing. They postpone living until some future retirement that may never come.
What, then, does a well-spent life look like? For the Stoic Seneca it meant dedicating time to contemplation and to the study of wisdom. Such study links a reader with the most illustrious minds of every era. A person who does so is not confined to his own brief span but can claim the whole of the past as his own.
Readers have long noted an irony: Seneca was among the wealthiest men in Rome and spent years at the imperial court as an adviser to Nero. Whether he lived up to his own precepts remains contested.

For more than a century new medicines have been tested on mice, rats, and monkeys before they reach human volunteers. Yet animals are imperfect proxies for people, and most drugs that enter human trials ultimately fail, often because of adverse effects that animal studies did not foresee. Researchers are now turning to organoids: minuscule clusters of human cells grown from stem cells that spontaneously organize themselves into rudimentary versions of organs such as the liver, the gut, or the brain. Because they are derived from human tissue, organoids can reveal toxic effects that might elude detection in a mouse. And because they can be grown from a particular patient's cells, they let physicians gauge how that person might respond to a treatment. Lawmakers and regulators have taken heed. In 2022 the United States abolished a long-standing statutory requirement that new drugs be tested on animals. In 2025 the Food and Drug Administration announced a plan to phase out animal testing for certain kinds of new drugs, beginning with a class of treatments widely known as monoclonal antibodies. Organoids nonetheless have shortcomings. They lack blood vessels and immune cells, and they cannot reveal how a drug circulates through an entire body. For now most scientists regard them as an adjunct to animal studies rather than a wholesale replacement.

For decades broadcasters justified the scant coverage of women's sports with a facile claim: audiences were not interested. The events of 2024 rendered <u>that argument</u> untenable. In April the final of the American college basketball tournament for women drew an average of nearly 19 million television viewers, more than watched the men's final that year. Much of the attention converged on Caitlin Clark of the University of Iowa, whose record-breaking scoring had turned her into a household name. Yet the interest did not dissipate when her college career ended. Professional women's leagues in several sports reported larger crowds, escalating ticket prices, and new broadcasting deals. Researchers who study sports media contend that interest and coverage reinforce each other. When games are shown at convenient hours and promoted with the same zeal as men's events, audiences grow, which in turn induces networks to invest more. In this view the small audiences of the past reflected not indifference but invisibility: fans could hardly embrace athletes they never had a chance to see. Skeptics caution that a single star can produce an ephemeral surge, and that the real test is whether viewers remain steadfast once that star retires.

Many of us know the experience: a faint buzz against the thigh, a hand reaching into a pocket, and then the discovery that the phone did not vibrate at all, or is not even there. The sensation has become prevalent enough to earn a name, phantom vibration syndrome, although it is not a medical disorder. In one survey of staff at an American hospital, roughly two-thirds said they had felt such vibrations. Psychologists often explain the phenomenon with signal detection theory. The brain relentlessly sorts ambiguous sensations, such as the brush of fabric or a twitch of muscle, deciding whether each one is salient. When missing a real signal seems costly, as with an urgent message from a supervisor, the brain lowers its threshold and accepts more false alarms in exchange for fewer misses. People who feel anxious about their relationships or who check their phones compulsively appear to report phantom vibrations more often, which is consistent with <u>this account</u>. The illusion is not evidence of some defect in the senses. It reflects a perceptual system trained perhaps too well by the very device it is waiting for. Some users say the sensations diminish once they keep the phone in a bag instead of a pocket.

In my first year out of college money was tight, so I canceled a long-planned trip but kept buying my favorite lipstick. When the economy declines, households defer buying cars, cancel vacations, and make do with worn-out furniture. Yet some observers have claimed that spending on small luxuries holds steady or even rises in such periods, an idea known as the lipstick effect. Leonard Lauder, then the chairman of the cosmetics company Estée Lauder, is often credited with popularizing the notion after noticing unusually strong lipstick sales during the economic downturn of 2001. The proposed logic is psychological. When a large purchase is out of reach, a modest indulgence confers a sense of gratification and control at a price most people can still afford. Some commentators have extrapolated the idea to other affordable treats, such as nail polish, chocolate, or a night at the cinema. Yet the evidence is mixed. Scrutiny of sales data suggests the pattern appears in some recessions but not in others. Critics point out that a theory malleable enough to explain rising sales of almost any inexpensive product is difficult to test. Still the concept endures, perhaps because it captures something many shoppers recognize in themselves: the impulse to buy a small reward when their larger hopes are put on hold for a while.

In 1851 London hosted the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, the forerunner of a long line of international fairs. Prince Albert, the husband of Queen Victoria, was among its most ardent promoters. The edifice that housed the event became as renowned as anything on display. It was designed by Joseph Paxton, a gardener who had earlier built large greenhouses for the Duke of Devonshire. It was made almost entirely of cast iron and glass. Assembled from standardized prefabricated parts, the structure rose in Hyde Park in a matter of months. The magazine Punch nicknamed it the Crystal Palace. More than six million visits were recorded before the exhibition closed in October. Visitors could scrutinize steam engines, printing presses, and commodities from distant colonies. For a penny they could also use flushing public toilets, a novelty at the time. The exhibition yielded a handsome profit. It was used to buy land in South Kensington, where several museums including the future Victoria and Albert Museum were later built. The Crystal Palace itself was taken down and rebuilt in south London, where it remained a perennial attraction until it burned down in 1936.

The vanilla that flavors ice cream and cakes comes from the long pods of a climbing orchid that originally grew only in the forests of Mexico and Central America. Measured by weight, it is one of the costliest spices on earth. The reason lies less in rarity than in labor. Each flower opens for only a single day, and unless it is pollinated within those hours, it withers without producing a pod. In Mexico native insects perform this task, but they did not travel with the plant. When colonial planters carried vanilla vines to islands in the Indian Ocean, the vines flourished and bloomed, yet they bore almost no fruit. The problem was solved in 1841 on the island of Reunion by Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy who devised a quick way to pollinate each flower by hand with a thin stick and his thumb. Growers still use his method, flower by flower, on almost every plantation. Even then, the pods need about nine months to ripen and several more months of sweating and drying in the sun before they develop their familiar aroma. As a result most vanilla flavor sold today comes from vanillin made cheaply in factories, and the natural spice remains a luxury.

Every working day in Mumbai some 200,000 lunchboxes travel from home kitchens to offices across the city and back again, carried by delivery workers known as dabbawalas. The service has operated for more than a century. What renders it remarkable is how little technology it relies on. Each box is inscribed with a concise code of colors, letters, and numbers showing where it was collected, which railway station it passes through, and where it must be delivered. Many of the workers have had scant formal schooling, yet errors are exceedingly rare. The dabbawalas demonstrate that a complex operation can run smoothly ____.

When a new safety device is introduced, people sometimes respond by taking more risks, a pattern researchers call risk compensation. Some studies have suggested that drivers with anti-lock brakes tended to drive more aggressively. They followed other cars more closely, as if spending part of the added protection on extra risk. How strong this effect is remains contentious, and few experts conclude safety equipment should therefore be abandoned. Still, the idea serves as an invaluable reminder that ____.

Stars seem to twinkle, but the flicker has nothing to do with the stars themselves. As their light passes through the atmosphere, it crosses pockets of air of slightly different temperature and density. Each pocket bends the light a little, and with the air always in motion, the bending changes many times a second. A star is so distant that it appears as a single point, so even a tiny shift makes it seem to waver. Planets usually shine steadily for a related reason: because they are much closer and appear as small disks rather than points, ____, leaving their overall glow almost unchanged.

When The Jazz Singer opened in 1927 with scenes of synchronized speech and song, audiences were captivated, and within a few years Hollywood had all but abandoned silent films. The change was not welcome to everyone. Some stars of the silent era had voices or accents that did not suit the new medium, and their careers declined rapidly. Cameras that had previously moved freely were at first confined inside soundproof booths to keep their noise off the soundtrack, and many early sound films looked static as a result. In other words, the arrival of sound ____. Only after quieter cameras and movable microphones arrived did filmmakers regain much of the freedom they had lost.

The QR code, now printed on everything from restaurant menus to train tickets, was not originally designed for consumers at all. The Japanese company Denso Wave developed it in 1994 to track automotive components in factories. Workers there needed a code that could hold more information than a conventional barcode and be scanned quickly from any angle. Because the company chose not to exercise its patent rights, other firms were free to adopt the format. Outside Japan the codes remained a niche technology for many years. Only when ordinary smartphone cameras could read them without a separate app did they ____. Today scanning one is as unremarkable as tapping a card to pay.

On a sweltering day most people reach for an iced drink rather than a cup of hot tea. Research in exercise physiology suggests the tea may sometimes be the better choice. A hot drink adds a little heat to the body, but it also prompts the skin to release noticeably more sweat. In a 2012 study, cyclists stored less heat after drinking hot water than after drinking cold water, since the extra sweat evaporated and carried warmth away. The benefit vanishes in humid air or under heavy clothing, where sweat cannot evaporate. Paradoxically, the lesson is that ____.

Koalas spend most of their lives asleep or resting, often for as long as twenty hours a day. Visitors sometimes presume that the animals are drugged by chemicals in eucalyptus leaves, but the real explanation lies in the poor quality of their diet. Eucalyptus leaves are tough, low in nutrients, and laced with compounds that are toxic to most mammals. Koalas rely on an elongated digestive tract and specialized gut microbes to process them, and the effort yields comparatively little energy. By sleeping for much of the day, koalas ____. In short, rest is how they balance a meager energy budget.

When a garment can no longer be sold or worn, it usually ends up in a landfill or an incinerator. Upcycling offers an alternative fate. Conventional recycling often shreds discarded clothes into low-grade fibers. Upcyclers instead turn them into products of equal or greater value: a heap of tattered denim becomes a patchwork jacket, and offcuts swept from a factory floor become a limited batch of bags. A number of luxury houses and many small independent labels now retail upcycled lines, and the approach has gained momentum as governments tighten regulations on textile waste. France, for instance, has required clothing brands since 2007 to help pay for the collection and recycling of the garments they sell. Yet upcycling faces a formidable obstacle: it is difficult to scale. Because every discarded garment varies in size, color, and condition, each item must be scrutinized, dismantled, and redesigned largely by hand. That makes the clothes expensive to produce and hard to standardize, so skeptics doubt that upcycling alone can absorb more than a modest share of the clothing thrown away each year. Its proponents counter that its real value may lie elsewhere: in persuading consumers to regard old clothes as raw material rather than trash.

Tell an adolescent that a particular film is unsuitable for her, and you may have just guaranteed that she will watch it. Psychologists call this response reactance, a term introduced by Jack Brehm in the 1960s. In his theory people believe they possess certain freedoms such as the freedom to choose what to read, eat, or think. When one of those freedoms is threatened, they experience a distressing state that drives them to restore it, often by doing precisely what they were forbidden to do. The prohibited option suddenly looks more alluring, and the person who imposed the restriction appears less credible. Reactance helps explain why heavy-handed public campaigns can backfire. Messages laden with commands such as "you must" or "stop now" tend to provoke stronger resistance than messages that offer reasons and leave the final decision to the audience. The effect is not universal; it varies with how important the threatened freedom is and how legitimate the source of pressure seems. But the lesson for parents, physicians, and advertisers is fairly consistent: if you want people to change their behavior, ____.

When schools around the world closed their doors in 2020, few people anticipated that the effects would persist for years. Yet when researchers assessed students' progress after classrooms reopened, many children had lagged well behind where earlier students had been at the same age. The deficits were generally larger in mathematics than in reading. The damage was not evenly distributed. Students from low-income families lost the most ground, since they were less likely to have a quiet place to study, reliable internet access, or an adult to help at home. This widened disparities dating from before the pandemic. Governments responded with emergency initiatives. One approach garnering particular attention was high-dosage tutoring, in which trained tutors meet small groups of students several times a week during the school day. Studies conducted before the pandemic had shown unusually large gains from such programs, but expanding them rapidly proved arduous: schools struggled to recruit enough tutors and to fit sessions into packed timetables. Meanwhile chronic absenteeism surged in the United States and elsewhere, and children who are not in class cannot benefit from supplementary help. In the United States national test results released in early 2025 showed that average reading scores had declined further rather than recovering. Many educators now contend that recovery will require sustained endeavor over many years.

For much of the twentieth century, chemists presumed they understood why slicing an onion makes people cry. Damaging the bulb, they reasoned, allowed a single enzyme to decompose sulfur compounds stored inside it, and the irritating vapor drifting up to the eyes then formed spontaneously from the products of the reaction. But in 2002 a team of Japanese scientists reported in the journal Nature that this account was incomplete. The vapor, they showed, does not simply appear on its own; a second, previously unknown enzyme is required to generate it. The finding mattered for more than scientific tidiness. It meant the tear-inducing gas and many substances giving onions their pungent taste arise from distinct steps, so in principle one might be diminished without losing the other. Researchers soon put the hypothesis to the test. By silencing the gene for the newly identified enzyme, scientists in New Zealand and Japan cultivated onions that released far less of the irritant when cut. The change also altered the onions' chemistry in other ways, elevating the levels of certain sulfur compounds linked to flavor. For cooks who would rather not weep over a cutting board, the work offered hope; for biologists, it was a reminder that even the most commonplace kitchen experience can conceal uncharted chemistry.

The shopping cart is so mundane that we easily forget it had to be invented. The first version was introduced in 1937 by Sylvan Goldman, owner of an Oklahoma City supermarket chain. It was fundamentally a folding chair on wheels carrying two baskets. It solved a genuine problem, since shoppers were prone to stop buying once a hand-held basket grew cumbersome, but it spawned new ones. Each cart had to be unfolded before use and folded again afterward, and stores needed space to accommodate them all. The decisive improvement came in the late 1940s, when an inventor named Orla Watson patented a cart with a hinged rear panel that swung open, letting one cart slide snugly into the next. Long rows of nested carts could now be stored in a fraction of the space, and the design became the norm worldwide after decades of refinement. Carts have since grown substantially larger, and retail analysts often speculate that this is no accident: a big basket that looks half empty may subtly encourage shoppers to keep filling it. Many stores, especially in Europe, also equip their carts with coin locks. Customers must insert a coin to release a cart and get the coin back only when they return the cart to its row.

"Strike it on your knee, then hold it near your ear." That was all the note said. It had come with a small steel tuning fork in a padded envelope sent by the nephew of Mrs. Arden, my old piano teacher, who had died the month before. According to his short letter, she had asked that the fork be sent to me. I could not fathom why. I had been her least promising student. I practiced grudgingly, mistook speed for proficiency, and quit abruptly at sixteen, telling her that music was a waste of time I could no longer afford. She did not argue. She only tapped the fork against the lid of the piano and said that every note I would ever play, or refuse to play, would still be measured against <u>that one</u>. That evening I struck the fork on my knee as instructed. A thin, steady tone permeated the quiet kitchen and before I knew it I was humming along, then searching for the same pitch on the cheap keyboard my daughter had abandoned in the hall closet. My fingers were stiff and clumsy. But for the first time in twenty years I was playing to impress no one, and even the scales sounded almost forgiving. I suspect she foresaw that I would come back eventually. She simply chose not to say so.
